The Great Divergence

Why here, why then

The best unsettled argument in economics, and every industrial policy implicitly picks a side.

2 min read3 figures, each sourcedWhere it is contestedCorrected onceUpdated 21 September 2026
On this pageBy the numbersHow it happenedWho did the workWhere it is contestedCorrectedWhat I changed my mind aboutGo to the sourceReads across to

For most of history, living standards barely moved. Then, in one corner of one continent, they did — and the argument about why has not been settled in twenty-five years of trying.

If you keep one line

Don't ask which explanation is right. Ask which constraint binds in the case in front of you.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

The candidates are all partly right and mutually incompatible. Kenneth Pomeranz argued that Britain and the Yangzi delta were comparably developed until roughly 1750, and that coal in the right place plus New World land — 'ghost acreage' relieving the ecological ceiling — tipped the balance. Robert Allen argued it was relative prices: Britain had expensive labour and cheap energy, so labour-saving machines paid there and nowhere else, which explains why the spinning jenny was adopted in Lancashire and ignored in France.

Joel Mokyr argued for culture — a European Republic of Letters that made useful knowledge contestable, cumulative and public, and an Industrial Enlightenment connecting the people who theorised to the people who built. Then there are institutions (Acemoglu and Robinson's inclusive property rights and constrained executives), demography and human capital (Gregory Clark's downward mobility of the rich), and the material of empire, slavery and coerced trade, whose contribution to European capital formation is measured differently by different historians.

The methodological problem underneath is that these explanations are not independent. Cheap coal makes steam pay, which makes engineering knowledge valuable, which makes a culture of tinkering rewarding, which builds institutions that protect tinkerers. Every account can absorb the others as downstream effects. That's why twenty-five years of scholarship has narrowed the dating without settling the causation.

What makes this the right obsession is that the stakes are current. Every argument about industrial policy, energy prices, immigration or state capacity is an implicit bet on one of these explanations. If Allen is right, relative prices drive invention and energy costs are the policy lever. If Mokyr is right, the lever is who is allowed to argue with whom, and how cheaply ideas cross borders.

01By the numbers

~1750Pomeranz's dating of comparable European and East Asian development: Princeton University Press, 'The Great Divergence' (publisher's description)
38% / 2.5%Return on a spinning jenny, England vs France: Robert C. Allen, 'The Industrial Revolution in Miniature', Oxford Economics WP 375 (2007)
2000Pomeranz's book names the debate, unresolved a quarter-century later: Kenneth Pomeranz, 'The Great Divergence', Princeton University Press, 2000

02How it happened

  1. 1750Pomeranz's estimated point of rough parity between Britain and the most advanced regions of China.
  2. 1776Watt's separate-condenser engine goes commercial — economic only where coal is cheap and labour dear.
  3. 1800sBritish real wages and energy prices diverge sharply from continental and Asian comparators.
  4. 2000Pomeranz publishes 'The Great Divergence' and names the debate.
  5. 2009Allen's 'The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective' puts relative prices at the centre.
  6. 2016Mokyr's 'A Culture of Growth' makes the case for the market for ideas.

03Who did the work

Kenneth PomeranzHistorian of China who reframed the question by taking Asian development seriously as a baseline.
Robert C. AllenReconstructed centuries of wage and price series, then argued the invention followed the prices.
Joel MokyrArgues the decisive variable was a culture in which useful knowledge could be contested and shared.

04Where it is contested

Nearly all of it. Pomeranz's late-divergence dating has been challenged by wage, height and consumption data suggesting a gap opened earlier. Allen's price series are disputed at the seams. Clark's mechanism is the least accepted of the major accounts. Anyone who tells you it's solved is selling something.

05Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 6 · Sept 2026 · Three explanations.

The Great Divergence printed '3' as a figure — the explanations still standing. It was my own count, not a sourced number, and the entry itself discusses more than three. It is replaced by Robert Allen's estimate of the return on a spinning jenny: 38% in England against 2.5% in France.

06What I changed my mind about

I used to want a single cause and treated the debate as a horse race. I now think the honest position is that these are complements with a plausible feedback loop, and that the useful question isn't 'which one' but 'which one is the binding constraint in the case in front of me'.
